events.excerpt: Two threads here this month made me look at the same problem from both ends. In one , a holder has ATOM on UX Chain, which halted in July, and RoboMcGobo explained why the Hub can’t just release it: the escrow only opens when the other chain burns the voucher, and that chain makes no blocks. In the other, Akash’s proposal 346 (voting until 2 November) starts a migration that ends with akashnet-2 halting 90 days after a later cutover. So I went through ibc-go (v10.7.0, the version Gaia v29.0.1 runs; akashnet-2 runs v10.5.0, and the transfer code I cite is the same there) to list what has to happen before the last block, because after it nobody can fix anything from the other side. This is not about whether any chain should leave. It’s only about the tokens. Why tokens get stuck When a token leaves its home chain, it goes into that chain’s escrow for the channel and the other side mints a voucher. The escrow releases it only when a packet shows the voucher was burned, and that packet has to come from a live chain. Transfer channels can’t be closed. The transfer module rejects ChanCloseInit , so there is no close-and-settle step. Every packet, ack and timeout is checked through the counterparty’s light client, and the client has to be Active. events.excerpt: Ephemeral Rollup: The New “L1.5” of Ethereum TLDR; Ethereum’s core job has always been verifying state transitions. While rollups made that verification succinct, they at the same time hold their users’ state, which is why every rollup needs an exit. Native account abstraction ( EIP-8141 and related EIPs) and proof aggregation are making it practical to keep compute and state apart. We call this L1.5 , albeit it is perhaps more an architectural pattern than a layer. In the pattern we are talking about: a) The wallet keeps the user’s own state, b) L1 keeps the shared state and verifies every transition, and c) the compute in between is done by whoever takes the job without holding any state the next job needs, and d) state changes settle directly on L1. The idea is not new: Relayers, builders and keypers have already done parts of this kind of job, and FOCIL’s includers will be next. What is new is the timing, “now and next”, as this becomes practical to build. We aim only to give a rough conceptualization of it in this post. Introduction Ethereum first verified state transitions by re-executing them. Rollups added succinct verification, where a fraud or validity proof lets L1 accept a batch without re-executing it. But a rollup also holds its users’ state. The state is kept in th
events.headline: Ephemeral Rollup: The New "L1.5" of Ethereum

TL;DR Zyfai would run up to 10M USDC from the SLL, rebalanced daily across USDC lending venues on Ethereum, including Spark Blue Chip USDC. Two risk tiers, chosen by Spark. Over the last 90 days, net of a 5% Zyfai fee, Spark’s margin over the Sky Savings Rate would have been: conservative: 96 bps, 1.7x Spark Blue Chip USDC (57 bps) aggressive: 278 bps, 4.9x Spark Blue Chip USDC On 10M per year: about $96k (conservative) or $278k (aggressive), against about $57k from Spark Blue Chip USDC. Spark keeps custody: the Safe is owned by SPARK_PROXY . Zyfai can only move funds between allowlisted venues or back to the ALM Proxy. No controller change: inflow uses the existing transferAsset path with a 10M rate limit. 1. Why The SLL earns the difference between venue yield and the Sky Savings Rate (SSR). Spark Blue Chip USDC is today Spark’s direct USDC allocation on Morpho: about 19.6M, almost all from the ALM Proxy, in two markets (cbBTC 86% LLTV about 85%, wstETH 86% LLTV about 15%). events.excerpt: The Internet can feel invisible when everything is working normally. But when connectivity breaks, the many systems it depends upon become evident in an instant. Because Cloudflare’s global network handles more than 20% of the web’s traffic, it offers a unique perspective of how Internet traffic is behaving. When failures in infrastructure, power, policy, or security disrupt access to the Internet, Cloudflare Radar can observe the impact by monitoring traffic to our customers. Each quarter, we review the disruptions detected and annotated on Radar, highlighting what happened, where it happened, and the broader conditions that shaped each event. In this post, we examine the major categories of Internet disruptions observed during the third quarter of 2026, including government-directed shutdowns, power outages and natural disasters. Disruptions at a glance Between July and September, Internet disruptions were largely driven by failures in the systems the Internet depends on. Power grids failed in Cuba, Honduras, Guam, Ukraine, and several other countries. Natural disasters damaged electricity and telecommunications infrastructure from Nepal to Colombia. Government-directed shutdowns remained the most frequent source of disruption, driven largely by exam-related shutdowns in Iraq,
events.headline: What took the Internet offline in Q3 2026

events.excerpt: Update — October 30, 2026: Thank you to everyone who has participated in the PHP Capture the Flag challenge. We have received a strong response from the security research community, and the submissions have helped us harden our existing php2shell WAF protections and create new detections. Details of managed-rule changes are available in the Cloudflare WAF changelog . The CTF remains open. We encourage researchers to continue submitting materially distinct, reproducible bypasses through the Cloudflare HackerOne program. We will share further information and feedback as the challenge progresses. Thank you again for your contributions. Last week was one for the Internet security history books. First, eight eMudhra intermediate certificates were compromised , creating the possibility of forged certificates that could be used to impersonate servers. Then came php2shell : serious vulnerabilities in PHP, the runtime behind a large portion of the Web. Cloudflare worked around the clock as these events unfolded to protect our customers and help protect the Internet. events.excerpt: Hi all, I am Nemo Unus, the pseudonymous maintainer of Proof of One. It is an open-source, non-commercial design for polls with four properties: Every participant is a unique human. Nobody, including operators, can link answers to people. Every voter can verify their own recorded ballot. Anyone can recount the result from public data. Full disclosure first: most of the current design and code was drafted with a team of AI agents, disclosed in AGENTS.md. None of it has been reviewed by independent humans yet. That is why I am posting. Design in brief Enrolment, document. The phone reads an ICAO 9303 passport chip over NFC. It proves in zero knowledge that the chip data was signed by a document signer in a public tree of checked signers, without revealing the document. The reference circuit handles SHA-256 and RSA-2048 and has 577,678 constraints. Proving time on phones is not yet measured. The signers are checked against a published trust list of country signing certificates. The list holds references only and has a hash anyone can rebuild. The first version is built from the German master list: 113 of 186 chip-passport countries. Enrolment, person. The live face is matched to the chip photo inside an attested enclave. events.excerpt: Author: @adust09 from Nyx Foundation Abstract In this post, we will take stock of the challenges facing PQ P2P in the consensus layer. Ethereum consensus-layer networking has no adopted post-quantum migration profile. Replacing validator BLS signatures with leanXMSS does not update the networking identities and handshakes used by ENRs , Discovery v5 , libp2p Peer IDs, or QUIC/TLS. The migration has three linked targets: Discovery: ENR signatures, Discovery identity proofs, and Discovery key exchange. Connection key exchange: TLS 1.3 key agreement inside QUIC. Connection authentication: libp2p TLS identity binding and TLS CertificateVerify . The main constraints are structural: an ENR is limited to 300 bytes, a Discovery packet to 1,280 bytes, and hybrid key exchange does not provide PQ authentication. In practice, hash-based signatures are being promoted for consensus signatures, but the size limits of the P2P layer make lattice-based schemes the de facto standard candidates for networking. This inventory maps the required changes without selecting an algorithm, encoding, or activation schedule. This article is intended for developers working on the network layer and libp2p. Please feel free to send me your feedback. 1. Scope This post covers Ethereum CL networking over libp2p an
events.headline: Inventory of PQ P2P Migrations in the Consensus Layer

events.excerpt: Hi everyone, I’m Samuel, building Privara, a privacy-focused payment protocol on Stacks. We’ve completed our initial grant milestones and deployed a working mainnet payment flow. I’m now exploring how to extend its privacy model, particularly around selective disclosure. What’s implemented Privara currently uses secp256k1-based stealth-address derivation to generate one-time recipient addresses, reducing the ability to link payments through a persistent recipient address. The implementation also includes SIP-018-based payment authorization, sponsored transaction flows, and payment discovery mechanisms. These provide recipient-address privacy, not full transaction confidentiality. Amounts, transaction activity, and other on-chain metadata remain observable. What I’m exploring The next step is payment-scoped selective disclosure: allowing a recipient to share verifiable information about a specific payment with an auditor or counterparty without exposing unrelated payments or granting access to their entire wallet history. I’m considering a design where a recipient can generate a narrowly scoped disclosure package containing payment-specific evidence, potentially supported by encrypted payment metadata and cryptographic proofs. This is still research, not an implemented viewing-key
events.headline: Privara: Exploring payment-scoped selective disclosure for privacy on Stacks

We have remediated the issue, and we restored the model on September 9. We have confirmed that no other model hosted on Workers AI was affected. events.excerpt: Since Prague, execution-layer requests for validator exits and partial withdrawals go through a 504-byte contract at 0x00000961Ef480Eb55e80D19ad83579A64c007002 , hand-written for the geas assembler. At the end of every block the protocol makes a system call to it, and that call is consensus-critical: EIP-7002 requires a block whose call fails to be invalidated. We proved two properties of the deployed runtime bytes in Lean 4: The system call always succeeds, whatever the contract’s storage holds, and uses at most 210,000 of the 30,000,000 gas it is given. Requests leave in exactly the order they arrived. Over any valid history since the contract’s deployment, the committed submissions are exactly the emitted withdrawal requests followed by the entries still queued. Both are stated against Jaune, an executable semantics of the EVM and block processing, also written in Lean, and cover the Prague, Osaka, BPO1 and BPO2 forks. The proofs use no axioms beyond Lean’s standard three: propext , Classical.choice and Quot.sound . Before deployment, the contract had already been examined by four audits and a loop-bounded Halmos check . The results here connect the deployed bytes to Jaune’s block processing, with exact gas, and follow requests from submission to delivery across histories. The
events.headline: Lean verification of EIP-7002: system-call success and FIFO requests

events.excerpt: Research & Context The Community Staking Module (CSM) has lowered the financial barrier to staking, allowing permissionless operators to spin up nodes. However, infrastructure centralization remains a silent bottleneck. Due to home bandwidth constraints, power grid instability, or upfront hardware costs, a significant cohort of solo operators choose turn-key hosted infrastructure providers (such as cloud VPS providers) rather than hosting physical hardware at home. While hosted providers lower the technical barrier, they introduce severe correlated infrastructure risks. If a single cloud provider or staking-as-a-service host experiences an outage, a large block of Lido CSM validators could go offline or face correlated slashing penalties simultaneously. Conversely, true home staking provides maximum resilience but suffers from lower uptime SLAs. We need a framework that bridges this gap—improving the accessibility of home infrastructure while structuring guardrails around hosted deployments. events.excerpt: Disclosure: I’m the founder of bb84, the payments app that runs on this chain. Feedback, especially critical feedback, is very welcome. TL;DR We run an OP Stack rollup on Ethereum mainnet (chain ID 42069000, live since 2026-09-30) where L2 transactions carry no signatures at all . An account is the tip of a keccak-256 hash chain. Spending reveals the next preimage. A commit–reveal step binds each preimage to one transaction before the preimage becomes public. Inside the L2 the only cryptographic assumption is preimage resistance of keccak-256, which Grover reduces to about 2^128 work. No known quantum algorithm does better. ECDSA still appears at the L1 boundary, and the system has other trust assumptions (listed below). I’d like to discuss whether this is a sensible interim design for post-quantum payments on Ethereum L2s, and where it breaks. Accounts s_0 = keccak256("OP_OTA_SPEND_v1" ‖ spend_sk ‖ r) // per-account secret s_k = keccak256(s_{k-1}) // k = 1..N, N = 1000 by default C = s_N // public commitment address = trunc20(keccak256("OP_HASH_ADDR_v1" ‖ C)) A predeploy ( NullifierTree , 0x4200…0042) stores per address: lastReveal (initially C ), chainDepth (initially N ) and the set of spent nullifiers. Accounts are registered through an L1 deposit or by the system-side Stealt
events.headline: A hash-only rollup: OP Stack L2 accounts as Lamport-style hash chains, no ECDSA inside the L2

events.excerpt: A video player seeking to the middle of a movie asks for a few megabytes. Under our old range caching, that one request could make Cloudflare pull 128 MiB from the origin and move it between data centers, sometimes after the viewer had already left. Range requests are how large files get delivered, and caching them naively easily leads to wasted network bandwidth and wasted disk operations when running a CDN at scale. So we rebuilt how our cache handles them. For R2, Cloudflare's object storage, p99 time to first byte dropped by about half, and a follow-up improvement cut tiered cache traffic for R2 and similar workloads by about 6%. Today, we're making that new implementation available as Origin Range Requests , a self-service feature on all plans. There's no range size to tune and no need to contact support. Turn it on with a Cache Rule , and Cloudflare handles the rest. A request for part of a file An HTTP range request asks for part of a resource instead of the whole resource. The client sends a normal GET with a Range header: GET /movie.mp4 HTTP/1.1 Host: example.com Range: bytes=1048576-2097151 If the server supports the request, it returns 206 Partial Content and identifies the returned bytes with Content-Range : HTTP/1.1 206 Partial Content Content-Range: bytes 1048576-20
events.headline: Origin Range Requests: Serving large files without range-request tuning

events.excerpt: Today, Cloudflare is launching a post-quantum geographically restricted key manager in support of our Data Localization Suite (DLS) in closed beta. This new PQ GeoKey Manager is a cornerstone of Cloudflare’s data sovereignty solutions, making sure that a customer's decryption keys are only accessible in their chosen geography. GeoKey Manager implements this by wrapping each decryption key such that it can only be decrypted by Cloudflare servers that are located in the allowed geography. While general availability (GA) is planned for Q1 2027, today’s launch is an important milestone on our journey to support our customers’ data sovereignty goals while also migrating all Cloudflare products to post-quantum (PQ) cryptography . Governments, financial institutions, healthcare providers, and defense organizations process highly sensitive data that can remain sensitive for years or decades after it is produced. Encryption is often required to protect this data. When classical, public-key encryption is used, adversaries do not immediately need a quantum computer today to put that data at risk: they can store the ciphertext and retain them until quantum computers can break the public key cryptography protecting it — an attack strategy known as harvest now, decrypt later. events.excerpt: The Arbitrum Developer Guild was first introduced in January 2024 alongside the Arbitrum Expansion Program. We have published the first version of the Guild’s specification and it is available in the Arbitrum Foundation’s documentation. The Guild is an invite-only and merit-based program facilitated by the Arbitrum Foundation. Membership is assessed based on demonstrated proof of work on the core Arbitrum Protocol or other high-impact technical contributions to the ecosystem. Members must also demonstrate strong alignment with Arbitrum such that their company’s success substantially depends on Arbitrum winning. The Guild is currently funded through 2% of Net Protocol Revenue from Arbitrum Chains alongside 3% of the Priority Gas Auctions (PGA) and the Sequencer Fast Feed proceeds from Arbitrum One. There are more than 30 Arbitrum Chains who are already contributing to the Guild. Each member will receive an allocated percentage of the funding on a regular cadence. This funding is intended primarily as an additional incentive on top of the member’s core business revenue. With this framework now in place, we are pleased to announce the first member of the Arbitrum Guild: Offchain. events.excerpt: This release updates the Flare and Songbird codebase to AvalancheGo v1.14.2. The upgrade is optional but encouraged. It is backwards compatible with v1.14.0 and does not schedule any new fork times. Note: Coreth and Subnet-EVM are now grafted into the AvalancheGo tree — there is no separate coreth module anymore. Go import paths change from github.com/ava-labs/coreth/... to github.com/ava-labs/avalanchego/graft/coreth/... , which affects downstream tools that import Coreth packages. Building from source now requires Go 1.25.11 or later.

events.excerpt: OpenSSL 4.1.0 is a feature release adding significant new functionality to OpenSSL. This release incorporates the following potentially significant or incompatible changes: Added VC-WIN32-MSVC2013 and VC-WIN64A-MSVC2013 build targets to provide internal functions for bridging the gaps in C99 standard support that are present in MSVC 2013. Added optimized ML-DSA and ML-KEM NTT operations on ppc64le ; optimized ML-DSA operations on x86_64 ; AVX-512-optimized SHAKE x4 operations for ML-DSA on x86_64 ; AVX-512 and VAES optimizations for AES-CBC decryption on x86_64 . Changed tsget utility to use Net::Curl::Easy (from the Net-Curl CPAN distribution) instead of the abandoned WWW::Curl::Easy . Users who rely on tsget should install Net::Curl::Easy before upgrading. Dropped Windows-on-Itanium ( VC-WIN64I ) and Windows CE ( VC-CE ) targets from Configurations. Dropped no-ecdsa and no-ecdh options from Configure , as these options did not really disable the implementations. Use no-ec to disable the elliptic curve support. This release adds the following new features: Support for DTLS 1.3 ( RFC 9147 ). Refer to the ossl-guide-dtlsv13(7) manual page for details. events.excerpt: This is a quick release that postpones the Amsterdam fork on the Hoodi testnet, previously scheduled for Oct 26, 2026, 17:42:48 UTC. Hoodi node operators running v1.17.9 must upgrade before then. A new date will be set in a future release; other networks are unaffected. Snap sync now switches to snap/2 automatically once Amsterdam is active. Use --snap.v2=false or --snap.v2=true to force a protocol. Changes Cancel the Amsterdam activation on Hoodi ( #36001 ) Use snap/2 automatically once Amsterdam is active ( #35989 ) Optimize DUP/SWAP dispatch in the interpreter ( #35959 ) For a full rundown of the changes please consult the Geth 1.17.10 release milestone.
